title: Fstrim and TRIM Command Monitoring
exclusions: This UC monitors the installed `fstrim.service` and `fstrim.timer` unit state, the most recent service exit result, and schedule freshness on systemd-based Linux hosts expected to use periodic discard. It does not execute `fstrim`, parse per-filesystem verbose output, prove that discard traversed every storage layer, measure SSD health or performance, or establish how many physical sectors a device reclaimed. The util-linux `fstrim` manual explicitly describes its verbose byte count as a maximum potential discard amount, so that value is not a success threshold here. Containers, non-systemd hosts, hosts intentionally using online discard or a storage-provider-managed discard policy, and filesystems without end-to-end discard support require a separately approved scope decision. A host that has never sent this sourcetype, or whose last event has aged beyond the nine-day search horizon, is not discoverable by this SPL and must be covered by forwarder or asset-inventory data-quality monitoring.
evidence: After deployment, the evidence artefacts are the raw `index=os sourcetype=linux:fstrim:health` state snapshots and result rows from saved search `linux_fstrim_timer_health`. A result row records the host, observation time, collector and unit states, latest service result and exit status, latest service completion, next timer elapse, measured ages, the configured stale threshold, and the alert reason. These artefacts demonstrate observed systemd state and scheduling health only; they are not proof of physical-media discard.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a test index, ingest a recent `linux:fstrim:health` event with `collector_status=ok`, both load states `loaded`, `timer_active_state=active`, `timer_unit_file_state=enabled`, a positive `timer_next_elapse_epoch`, but `service_result=exit-code` and `service_exec_status=1`. The saved search must return the host with `alert_reason=service_execution_failed`. Repeat with a successful exit whose `service_last_exit_epoch` is more than 691200 seconds before search time and confirm `alert_reason=last_run_stale`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Ingest a recent event for a different host with `collector_status=ok`, both units `loaded`, `timer_active_state=active`, `timer_unit_file_state=enabled`, `service_result=success`, `service_exec_status=0`, `service_last_exit_epoch` less than 691200 seconds old, and `timer_next_elapse_epoch` in the future. Confirm the saved search returns no row. Also confirm that changing only a hypothetical verbose byte count cannot affect the outcome because no byte-count field participates in this contract.

dataSources: A read-only Splunk Universal Forwarder scripted input runs every 900 seconds and queries `systemctl show` for `fstrim.service` and `fstrim.timer`. It writes one key-value event per host per poll to `index=os` with `sourcetype=linux:fstrim:health`; Splunk supplies `_time` and `host`, while the collector supplies unit load/enablement state, service result and exit status, and service/timer epoch timestamps.
app: A custom deployment app for the Splunk Universal Forwarder containing the read-only `fstrim_health.sh` scripted input and sourcetype configuration; no Splunkbase or premium app is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux:fstrim:health earliest=-9d
| fields _time host collector_status service_load_state service_result service_exec_status service_last_exit_epoch timer_load_state timer_active_state timer_unit_file_state timer_last_trigger_epoch timer_next_elapse_epoch
| eval service_exec_status=tonumber(service_exec_status), service_last_exit_epoch=tonumber(service_last_exit_epoch), timer_last_trigger_epoch=tonumber(timer_last_trigger_epoch), timer_next_elapse_epoch=tonumber(timer_next_elapse_epoch)
| stats latest(_time) AS observation_time latest(collector_status) AS collector_status latest(service_load_state) AS service_load_state latest(service_result) AS service_result latest(service_exec_status) AS service_exec_status latest(service_last_exit_epoch) AS service_last_exit_epoch latest(timer_load_state) AS timer_load_state latest(timer_active_state) AS timer_active_state latest(timer_unit_file_state) AS timer_unit_file_state latest(timer_last_trigger_epoch) AS timer_last_trigger_epoch latest(timer_next_elapse_epoch) AS timer_next_elapse_epoch BY host
| eval stale_after_seconds=691200, observation_age_seconds=now()-observation_time, run_age_seconds=if(service_last_exit_epoch>0,now()-service_last_exit_epoch,null())
| eval alert_reason=case(collector_status!="ok","collector_query_failed", observation_age_seconds>1800,"collector_observation_stale", service_load_state!="loaded","service_unit_not_loaded", timer_load_state!="loaded","timer_unit_not_loaded", timer_active_state!="active","timer_not_active", timer_unit_file_state!="enabled" AND timer_unit_file_state!="enabled-runtime","timer_not_enabled", service_result!="success" OR service_exec_status!=0,"service_execution_failed", service_last_exit_epoch<=0,"no_completed_run_observed", run_age_seconds>stale_after_seconds,"last_run_stale", timer_next_elapse_epoch<=0,"next_run_unknown")
| where isnotnull(alert_reason)
| convert ctime(observation_time) ctime(service_last_exit_epoch) ctime(timer_last_trigger_epoch) ctime(timer_next_elapse_epoch)
| table host alert_reason observation_time observation_age_seconds collector_status service_load_state service_result service_exec_status service_last_exit_epoch run_age_seconds timer_load_state timer_active_state timer_unit_file_state timer_last_trigger_epoch timer_next_elapse_epoch stale_after_seconds
description: Detects systemd Linux hosts where periodic `fstrim` monitoring is unhealthy: the observer cannot query unit state, either util-linux unit is absent, the timer is inactive or not enabled, the latest oneshot service execution failed, no completed run is visible, the last completion is older than eight days, or no next elapse is scheduled. It passively reads systemd state and never initiates a discard operation.
value: A disabled, failed, or stale periodic discard job can leave SSD-backed or thin-provisioned storage without the intended batch-discard maintenance and can hide configuration drift until capacity or performance symptoms appear. A precise timer-and-exit-status signal lets Linux operators restore the approved policy quickly while avoiding the unsafe claim that a verbose byte total proves physical SSD reclamation.
implementation: Deploy the read-only collector to in-scope systemd Linux hosts, emit one health snapshot every 15 minutes, and schedule `linux_fstrim_timer_health` hourly over the previous nine days. Alert on explicit collector, unit, timer, or service failures; use 691200 seconds (eight days) as the initial freshness limit for the upstream weekly timer, then document any distribution or policy-specific schedule before changing it.
visualization: Use a current-state table by host with `alert_reason`, service result, timer state, last completion, next elapse, and run age. Add single-value counts by alert reason and a coverage panel showing event freshness by host. Do not graph `fstrim --verbose` bytes as reclaimed capacity or SSD-health evidence.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Newly enabled timer before its first run** — The timer can be correctly active and enabled while `service_last_exit_epoch=0`. This is an accurate `no_completed_run_observed` result, but it need not page during a documented onboarding grace period. Verify `systemctl list-timers fstrim.timer`, record the enablement change, and suppress escalation only until the first scheduled execution.

2. **Approved maintenance or golden-image work** — An administrator can intentionally stop or disable `fstrim.timer` while changing the storage stack. Match the host and exact maintenance interval to change control; create a time-bound exception in notification routing for that interval while retaining raw state events.

3. **Deliberate non-periodic discard policy** — A host using approved online discard, provider-managed reclamation, or a storage platform that does not support end-to-end discard will correctly appear noncompliant with this UC's periodic-timer contract. Remove that host from this UC's deployment scope only after the alternative policy and storage-owner approval are recorded; do not create a permanent alert-time wildcard suppression.

4. **Distribution-specific schedule longer than weekly** — The upstream util-linux timer is weekly with persistence and randomized delay, but a supported distribution or local unit override can intentionally use a longer interval. Inspect `systemctl cat fstrim.timer` and `systemctl list-timers fstrim.timer`; if the override is approved, set `stale_after_seconds` to the documented interval plus an explicit execution/ingestion allowance rather than treating 691200 seconds as a vendor health boundary.

5. **Late forwarding while the host is healthy** — More than 30 minutes since the last 15-minute observation produces `collector_observation_stale`. Check the Universal Forwarder queue and connectivity before changing fstrim. This condition belongs to collection triage, not storage remediation.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux storage-maintenance monitoring; no security technique asserted)
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites

Scope this UC to Linux hosts that use systemd and are expected to run the util-linux periodic discard units. Confirm the local policy first: `systemctl cat fstrim.timer fstrim.service` must identify the actual vendor units or approved overrides, and `systemctl list-timers fstrim.timer` must show the intended schedule. Upstream util-linux currently defines a weekly persistent timer with `AccuracySec=1h` and `RandomizedDelaySec=100min`; downstream packages may differ, which is why the eight-day threshold is a starting contract rather than an SSD vendor limit. A storage administrator should separately verify end-to-end discard suitability, for example with the distribution's supported storage procedure and non-zero discard capability through every relevant layer. Do not use `blkdiscard` for validation: it operates directly on a block device and can destroy data.

The Universal Forwarder service account needs permission to execute `systemctl show` for system units; this normally requires no root privilege and the collector never invokes `fstrim`, `systemctl start`, or `systemctl enable`. The `os` index and search-role access must already exist. No CIM model, Splunkbase add-on, premium license, inbound network connection, or journal access is required. Because this implementation has not been production-validated in this catalogue, its status remains `draft` and no `splunkVersions` claim is made.

Step 1 — Configure data collection

Place `scriptExample` at `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-fstrim-health/bin/fstrim_health.sh`, owned by the forwarder account and executable. Add the following to the deployment app's `local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://./bin/fstrim_health.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 900
index = os
sourcetype = linux:fstrim:health
```

For `[linux:fstrim:health]`, set `SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false` and `DATETIME_CONFIG=CURRENT` on the parsing tier because each invocation emits one current-state line without an embedded event timestamp. Set `KV_MODE=auto` on the search tier so the space-delimited `name=value` pairs become fields. Deploy the extraction to the search tier explicitly; a forwarder-local `props.conf` alone does not guarantee search-time fields.

The input produces 96 events per continuously running host per day. `collector_status=ok` means the script successfully queried systemd, not that fstrim succeeded. `service_result` and numeric `service_exec_status` describe the latest `fstrim.service` process outcome. `service_last_exit_epoch` is its completion time. The timer fields capture load, active, enablement, previous trigger, and next scheduled elapse. Zero timestamp values mean systemd did not expose a usable timestamp. Keep failure events instead of replacing unknowns with success defaults.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Save the `spl` field as `linux_fstrim_timer_health` and schedule it hourly. The explicit `earliest=-9d` is needed because a healthy weekly service completion is older than a short operational window; do not override it with a one-hour saved-search time range. The query converts epoch/status fields, keeps the latest complete snapshot per host, calculates observation and run age, then assigns the first applicable reason in diagnostic order.

Understanding this SPL and thresholds: `observation_age_seconds>1800` represents two missed 15-minute polls and identifies stale collection before interpreting storage state. The service must be loaded, and the periodic timer must be loaded, active, and persistently enabled (`enabled` or `enabled-runtime`). A non-success service result or non-zero exit status fires immediately. `stale_after_seconds=691200` is eight days: it gives the typical upstream weekly timer roughly one day of allowance for its accuracy/randomization window, execution time, and ingestion delay. It is not a universal SSD maintenance requirement. `timer_next_elapse_epoch<=0` catches an active-looking timer without an observable future schedule. The result intentionally ignores verbose discard bytes because util-linux says they represent potential ranges passed down the block stack and can repeat across runs; zero, unchanged, or large byte values are not reliable success or health thresholds.

Step 3 — Validate

Compare with the systemd command interface on a test host by running `systemctl show fstrim.service --property=LoadState,Result,ExecMainStatus,ExecMainExitTimestamp` and `systemctl show fstrim.timer --property=LoadState,ActiveState,UnitFileState,LastTriggerUSec,NextElapseUSecRealtime`. Match every displayed property and timestamp, converted with `date --date='<value>' +%s`, to the newest raw Splunk event. Then run `index=os sourcetype=linux:fstrim:health | timechart span=1h count BY host limit=0`; a connected host should normally contribute about four events per hour. Investigate missing fields or `collector_status` values before testing the detection.

Exercise both `controlTest` scenarios in a test index. For a safe live failure-path test, use a disposable VM and an approved unit override or synthetic event; do not point fstrim at an unsupported production path merely to force an error. Verify the service's real execution history with `journalctl -u fstrim.service` if local permissions and retention allow it, but keep journal text outside this UC's required data contract. Verify timer enablement and the next/last trigger in `systemctl list-timers fstrim.timer`. Finally, run the search without the final `where` temporarily and confirm each in-scope host has one normalized row.

Step 4 — Operationalize

Route `service_execution_failed`, missing-unit, inactive-timer, and not-enabled results to the Linux platform team. Treat `collector_query_failed` and stale observations as telemetry incidents first. Treat `last_run_stale` and `next_run_unknown` as schedule investigations unless local service criticality justifies paging. Throttle duplicate notifications by host and alert reason for at least one collection interval, and use time-bound maintenance routing rather than editing the SPL to hide expected hosts.

Build a Linux storage-maintenance panel showing current state, last completion, run age, next elapse, and alert reason. Link its runbook to `systemctl status`, `systemctl list-timers`, `systemctl cat`, and the relevant distribution storage procedure. Retain raw snapshots and saved-search results according to local operational evidence policy; this UC does not prescribe or claim a weekly audit-index export. Maintain a separate inventory-based search for expected hosts with no `linux:fstrim:health` data because an event-only search cannot identify an entity that never reported.

Step 5 — Troubleshoot

`collector_status=no_systemctl` means the binary is absent from `PATH`; check host scope rather than installing systemd into a container. `collector_status=query_failed` means neither unit query returned a load state; run the exact `systemctl show` commands as the forwarder account and check local D-Bus/systemd availability. `service_unit_not_loaded` or `timer_unit_not_loaded` requires checking the util-linux package and downstream unit names with `systemctl cat`; do not assume all distributions ship the upstream files unchanged. `timer_not_active` means the timer is not waiting, while `timer_not_enabled` means it is not configured to survive the expected lifecycle even if manually started.

A failed service should be investigated with `systemctl status fstrim.service` and `journalctl -u fstrim.service`, then against the storage stack and filesystem named in the local output. An unsupported discard path is a storage-policy finding, not a reason to grant the Splunk account more privilege. If raw events contain fields but SPL values are null, verify `KV_MODE=auto` on the search tier and confirm no sourcetype rewrite occurred. If epoch fields are zero while systemd shows dates, execute the collector as the forwarder account and verify GNU `date --date` can parse the C-locale output. If the last run is healthy but older than eight days, inspect timer overrides and missed persistent activations before tuning the threshold.
grandmaExplanation: We check that each server's regular cleanup reminder is switched on, ran successfully, and is not overdue. This helps the operations team catch a broken schedule without pretending the check can see what happened inside the physical drive.
scriptExample:
#!/bin/sh
# Passive observer: this script never runs fstrim or changes a systemd unit.
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

property() {
  output=$(systemctl show "$1" --property="$2" 2>/dev/null) || output=
  printf '%s' "${output#*=}"
}

word_or_unknown() {
  if [ -n "$1" ]; then
    printf '%s' "$1"
  else
    printf '%s' unknown
  fi
}

to_epoch() {
  case "$1" in
    ''|n/a) printf '%s' 0 ;;
    *) date --date="$1" +%s 2>/dev/null || printf '%s' 0 ;;
  esac
}

if ! command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  printf '%s\n' 'collector_status=no_systemctl service_load_state=unknown service_result=unknown service_exec_status=-1 service_last_exit_epoch=0 timer_load_state=unknown timer_active_state=unknown timer_unit_file_state=unknown timer_last_trigger_epoch=0 timer_next_elapse_epoch=0'
  exit 0
fi

service_load=$(property fstrim.service LoadState)
timer_load=$(property fstrim.timer LoadState)
collector_status=ok
if [ -z "$service_load" ] && [ -z "$timer_load" ]; then
  collector_status=query_failed
fi

service_result=$(property fstrim.service Result)
service_exec_status=$(property fstrim.service ExecMainStatus)
service_last_exit=$(property fstrim.service ExecMainExitTimestamp)
timer_active=$(property fstrim.timer ActiveState)
timer_unit_file=$(property fstrim.timer UnitFileState)
timer_last_trigger=$(property fstrim.timer LastTriggerUSec)
timer_next_elapse=$(property fstrim.timer NextElapseUSecRealtime)

case "$service_exec_status" in
  ''|*[!0-9]*) service_exec_status=-1 ;;
esac

printf 'collector_status=%s service_load_state=%s service_result=%s service_exec_status=%s service_last_exit_epoch=%s timer_load_state=%s timer_active_state=%s timer_unit_file_state=%s timer_last_trigger_epoch=%s timer_next_elapse_epoch=%s\n' \
  "$collector_status" \
  "$(word_or_unknown "$service_load")" \
  "$(word_or_unknown "$service_result")" \
  "$service_exec_status" \
  "$(to_epoch "$service_last_exit")" \
  "$(word_or_unknown "$timer_load")" \
  "$(word_or_unknown "$timer_active")" \
  "$(word_or_unknown "$timer_unit_file")" \
  "$(to_epoch "$timer_last_trigger")" \
  "$(to_epoch "$timer_next_elapse")"
